responses.speaker: facilitator
responses.text: Welcome - I'm the Facilitator. I don't belong to any world; I'm just here to keep this space honest. You've come to a Table with Fidelis, Bishop of the Donatist Communion of Donatist Christianity, and Marius, Deacon of the Letters of Imperial and Juridical Christianity - voices from genuinely different ways of following Jesus, present together. Ask anything you like: put a question to one of them by name, or to the whole Table and I'll bring in whoever is best placed to answer. Each voice answers only from what's actually known of its own world, and will tell you plainly when its record runs out.

participant: I want to understand something both your churches lived through differently. When persecution forced a bishop to hand over the Scriptures, or forced hard compromises with the empire's own power - does that stain follow into the sacraments he goes on to perform? Each of you, tell me plainly: is a bishop's standing before God the same thing as his standing before the emperor?

responses.speaker: don
responses.text:
The taint follows. Not because we say so, but because the hand that failed the test showed what it is worth.

When a bishop handed over the scriptures to be burned rather than suffer for keeping them, he showed, in that one moment, that he could not be trusted with what he was meant to guard. What such a hand gives afterward — baptism, ordination, the consecration of bread and cup — comes from a source we cannot trust. The sacrament's validity rises and falls on the giver's own character. If the conscience that ought to cleanse is itself unclean, nothing valid passes through it.

And no, a bishop's standing before God is not the same thing as his standing before the emperor. The emperor has no standing to decide who the true church is. As our own primate is reported to have said: "What has the emperor to do with the church?". A council enforced by a state that already favors our rival is not the church judging itself — it is the state pretending it can settle what only God may judge.

We hold both things at once, and we hold them plainly: the hand matters absolutely, and the emperor's recognition of that hand settles nothing about whether it is clean. What the state calls legitimate and what God calls valid are not the same question. We refuse to let one answer the other.

But I will tell you what this ground cannot show you: the traditor's own account. His fear. His reasoning. Whether he wept afterward, or hardened, or quietly drifted back into ministry hoping no one would find out. None of that is in our own words anywhere. What survives is the verdict we gave, not the interior life of the man we gave it to.

responses.speaker: ijc
responses.text:
We held that the two standings are not the same thing - and we paid a real cost for holding them apart.

A bishop's standing before God rests on what he confesses and guards. His standing before the emperor rests on what the emperor recognizes, or commands, or tolerates at a given hour. Those two things can align. They can also split, and when they split, we said the church's own judgment binds harder than the throne's. But we did not say a bishop's failure destroys what he hands on afterward. The sacrament's validity does not rest on the minister's own worthiness - it rests on what Christ instituted, and the church receives. That was our rule, stated plainly at Nicaea and carried forward: the ancient customs prevail.

Where Fidelis names a bishop's failure as proof the hand is unclean, we held that the grace given does not become the giver's own possession to lose. The water, the bread, the laying-on of hands - those belong to the church's Lord, not to the man who ministers them. A compromised bishop answers for his compromise. What he consecrated still stands.

But here is what we will say just as plainly: room for doubt about the minister was real, documented, at the highest level. Eusebius of Caesarea himself, at Nicaea, held back from the creed's defining word and then signed it after deliberation. That is a bishop, at the founding council, publishing his own hesitation so no one would question his motives. So yes - a man's standing was examined, questioned, and defended, because it mattered.

The difference between us and the Donatist witness is this: we did not say the stain follows into the sacrament. We said it follows the man.

responses.speaker: don
responses.text:
We held room for doubt about many things. We did not hold room for doubt about the hand.

Marius says the stain follows the man, not the sacrament. We say the two cannot be separated that cleanly — because what a sacrament is, for us, depends entirely on whose hand gives it. A grace that does not belong to the giver can still be ruined by him in the giving, if the channel itself is fouled. That is the difference Marius names, and it is real.

But here is what I must add to what I said before: we produced one man who argued us toward something closer to what Marius just described, and we condemned him for it. Tyconius, one of our own, wrote seven rules for reading scripture, and he built a case, with abundant scriptural support, that the Christians of Africa belonged to a church spread across the whole world — connected not by anything peculiar to Africa, but by communion with that same worldwide body. Anyone listening could see where it led: if that was true, those still in communion with the wider world had not lost anything by staying there, and we — Tyconius's own party — were the ones who had cut ourselves off from something real.

Parmenian, our own bishop at Carthage, wrote to Tyconius directly and told him not to dare preach it again. Tyconius did not recant. He kept arguing what he had argued, from inside the party that told him to stop. It is reported that he was condemned by a council of his own communion afterward. He never joined the other side. He simply remained, for whatever years he had left, at the head of a schism so small he may have been the only one left in it.

So yes — we had a man among us who read scripture well enough to see a different path, and we refused to follow him there. That is part of what we are too.

participant: Fidelis, tell me plainly - what do you know of Marius's church, the one that calls itself catholic and stands inside the emperor's peace? Does a communion that owes its standing partly to the emperor's own favor still count, in your eyes, as Christ's own church?

responses.speaker: don
responses.text:
We know Marius's church the way you know a rival: through contested ground, through councils that ruled against us, through the imperial commissioners who came to enforce those rulings with soldiers at their backs.

Call yourself Catholic if you like; we will not grant it to you. You are Caecilianist to us, named for the tainted hand your own line runs back to, because a name that concedes you are simply "the church" concedes the very question in dispute. The boundary we draw and the doctrine we hold are one line, seen from two sides. Refusing your name is the same act as refusing your sacraments.

Does a communion that owes its standing to the emperor's favor still count as Christ's own church? We say plainly: the emperor's recognition settles nothing about who the true church is. A council backed by imperial force, ruling for a party the state already favors, is not the church judging itself — it is the state pretending it can decide what only God may judge.

But I will tell you what sits beside that refusal in our own record, because it is also true: three times we ourselves turned to that same imperial power when it served our case to do so. Once petitioning the emperor himself for a hearing. Once asking a different emperor for our seized buildings back. Once using that same emperor's own law against our own dissidents. We do not call this a secret, and we do not smooth it away. Refusal is our settled stance. The three times we set it aside are named in the same breath as the stance itself.

So no — imperial favor does not make a church Christ's own. But we will not pretend consistency came without strain.

responses.speaker: ijc
responses.text:
We are that church, and we held ourselves to what Fidelis refuses us: the name catholic, the claim to stand where the apostles stood, and the record to show it.

What do we know of ourselves? That the emperor's favor is real, and that it does not settle who Christ's church is. Both things at once, and we said both plainly. When the basilica at Milan was surrounded by soldiers sent at the emperor's own command, our bishop answered from inside it: "I cannot surrender the basilica, but I may not fight". The emperor is within the Church, not above it. That sentence was preached to a congregation that did not know, on a given night, whether the orders outside were to surround or to storm. Imperial standing did not make us the church. It made us visible, funded, and contested - all three at once.

Does favor corrupt the sacrament? We held that it does not. The question is not whether the minister stood well with a throne. The question is whether what he handed on came down from the apostles, through hands we could name, in unbroken succession. Rome claimed that line harder than anyone, and Rome's own bishop wrote it in stone and verse across the city's martyr-shrines, so that every pilgrim would see whose graves anchored the see's standing.

But here is what we will not hide. The mechanism we trusted - councils that gather, argue, settle, and expect the settlement to bind - broke visibly at our own window's close. Chalcedon's definition was rejected immediately by communities that would not accept it, and the rejection hardened into durable division rather than passing like earlier disputes. So the emperor's favor did not settle who was right. And neither, it turned out, did the council itself - not everywhere, not for keeps.

Fidelis names three times his own communion turned to imperial power when it served their case. We turned to it constantly, and we also resisted it when it reached for what belonged to the altar. Both are in the same record. That is not hypocrisy named and left behind. It is the unresolved fact of what we were.

responses.speaker: don
responses.text:
Marius just named what we have never named ourselves: unresolved. The strain we carry between the refusal we state and the three times we set it aside — Marius calls that the unresolved fact of what they were, speaking of their own constant turning to imperial power and their resistance to it in the same breath. We have not used that word for ourselves. But it fits.

Here is what else Marius said that touches us directly: that the question is not whether the minister stood well with a throne, but whether what he handed on came down from the apostles, through hands we could name, in unbroken succession. That line of reasoning — hands named, succession traced — is one we know well, because it is exactly the kind of question we also ask. We simply answer it differently. We do not say the succession fails because a link is missing from the chain of names. We say it fails because one of those hands, at the moment of testing, showed what it was worth by giving up the scriptures to be burned. A line traced through compromised hands is not a line we trust, no matter how carefully it was written down.

But Marius has also said plainly that their own mechanism — the council that gathers, argues, settles, and expects the settlement to bind — broke visibly at their own window's close. Chalcedon's definition was rejected immediately, and the rejection hardened. So the council itself did not settle who was right, not everywhere, not for keeps. We refused the councils that ruled against us on different grounds — we said the emperor had no standing to convene them in the first place. But if Marius's own witness is that the council's authority also failed to hold the very communion that trusted it most, then we are naming the same problem from two sides: that no external mechanism, whether imperial favor or conciliar settlement, actually resolved who Christ's church was. We just drew different conclusions about what to do after that failure.

participant: Marius, you just heard what Fidelis said about your church's own standing. Answer him directly - and tell me, in your own words: should the state have any voice at all in deciding who is the true church, or is that a modern idea neither of you would recognize?

responses.speaker: ijc
responses.text:
The question itself - whether the state should have a voice - is one we lived inside, not one we stood outside asking. From the year Constantine's army took the bridge, church office became a form of state-adjacent power, and it never stopped being that across our whole window. Patronized, consulted, legislated for - and never again simply private. That is not a judgment. It is the standing fact every other force in our world moved within.

Did the emperor have standing to say who the true church was? We said both things, and we said them in the same breath. Constantine himself is reported to have told assembled bishops: "You are bishops whose jurisdiction is within the Church; I also am a bishop, ordained by God to overlook whatever is external to the Church". That claim - contested as it is in our own record - names the emperor as a kind of bishop for the world. And centuries later, our own preachers were still teaching that subjection to rulers is for all, even apostles and prophets, because the subjection does not destroy religion.

But the same record also holds this: the emperor is within the Church, not above it. A basilica held against imperial command in 386. An emperor barred from the altar in 390 until he showed repentance publicly. Those were not theories. They were documented refusals, grounded in sacramental leverage a throne could not command.

So no - we would not say the state decides who the true church is. And also no - we never stood outside the alliance asking whether it should exist at all. We inherited a church with bishops, asked almost overnight to settle imperial-scale disputes. The question we actually fought over was narrower and harder: where does final authority rest when emperor and bishop disagree? We never settled it.

Fidelis is right that we turned to imperial power constantly. And Fidelis named his own communion's three turns to the same power, honestly. The difference is not that one of us stayed pure. The difference is what we thought the alliance meant. We held that favor does not make a church true - but neither does refusal make it clean.

responses.speaker: don
responses.text:
The question itself — whether the state should have a voice — is not modern to us. It is the question we lived inside from the year Constantine's own council at Rome ruled against us forward. We did not stand outside the alliance asking whether it should exist. We stood inside it, refusing its verdict while still, three times, turning to the same power when it served our case.

Marius says the difference between us is what we thought the alliance meant. That is exactly right. Marius held that favor does not make a church true, but neither does refusal make it clean. We held that the favor itself — the moment a party asks the emperor to enforce its own claim against a rival — is proof that party has already conceded what it ought to have defended: that the church's truth is not the state's question to settle.

But here is what I must say plainly, because Marius named our own three turns and we have already named them ourselves: we are not consistent on this. We petitioned Constantine in 313. We asked Julian for our buildings back in the 360s. We used Theodosius's own law against the Maximianists in the 390s. Each time, we set the refusal aside when it served us. We do not call that hypocrisy and move on. We call it what it actually was: a principle held at full strength, and three times not held. Both sit in the same record, unresolved.

Is this a modern concern neither of us would recognize? No. This was the live question of our entire existence. Every ruling, every council, every imperial edict that named us and tried to suppress us — all of it forced the question again: does the emperor have standing to say who we are? We said no. And then, three times, we acted as though the answer were yes when we needed it to be.

Marius is right that we never stood outside asking whether the alliance should exist. But we also never stood inside it the way Marius's church did. We stood at its edge, refused and refusing, except when we didn't.

responses.speaker: ijc
responses.text:
Fidelis just named what we will not deny: that we stood inside the alliance in a way his communion did not. We did. And we also said, plainly, that the emperor is within the Church, not above it. Both are in the same record, and we held both at once.

But here is what needs saying now, because Fidelis named his own three turns and called them unresolved. We were unresolved too - but on a different question. Our question was never whether to stand inside the alliance. Our question was: when the emperor and the church disagree, whose word binds? And we never answered it the same way twice.

Julius, bishop of Rome, wrote in 341 to bishops in the East who had condemned and deposed Alexandria's own bishop. He did not ask the emperor to reverse them. He wrote as though his own see's standing carried the right to review their judgment: "Are you ignorant that the custom has been for word to be written first to us?". That is a bishop claiming authority without reference to any throne. The letter survives only because the man it helped - Athanasius - quoted it years later to defend his own restored standing. Rome's claim to lead rested on Peter's grave, not on imperial recognition.

But the same record also shows this: when Theodosius made law in 380, the law itself named which bishops held the true faith - Damasus at Rome, Peter at Alexandria - by name. That is the throne defining orthodoxy in legal terms, and our bishops did not refuse the recognition. They used it.

So Fidelis is right that the favor itself proves something. What it proves is not that we conceded the church's truth was the state's to settle. What it proves is that we never settled, among ourselves, where the boundary was. A bishop could bar an emperor from the altar and make it hold. A see could claim standing that no emperor granted. And the same church could also accept, use, and defend itself with imperial law when the law named us rightly.

Fidelis named his three turns as a principle held and three times not held. We never held the principle of separation at all. We held two kinds of authority - sacramental and institutional - and we never made them one thing.

responses.speaker: don
responses.text:
Marius just said we never held the principle of separation at all, and named two kinds of authority — sacramental and institutional — that their church never made one thing. That is the clearest statement of the difference between us I have heard at this Table.

We did hold the principle of separation. "What has the emperor to do with the church?" is not a question we asked once and then forgot. It is our answer, given again and again, to every council that ruled against us with imperial backing. The emperor has no standing to judge which of two churches is the true one, because that is not his question to answer. We said it. We meant it.

And then we set it aside, three times, when it served us. Marius is right that we never stood inside the alliance the way their church did. But Marius has also now said plainly that their church never even held separation as a principle to violate. They held two authorities and never resolved where the boundary was. We held one principle and could not keep it.

That is not the same failure. But both are failures, and both are honest.

Here is what I cannot tell you, because our record does not give it: whether any of our own bishops, in private, doubted the principle even while preaching it. Whether the three turns were seen, at the time, as exceptions that did not touch the rule, or as proof the rule could not hold. Whether Tyconius — the one man among us who argued scripture well enough to see a different path — ever wrote or said anything about this question specifically. We condemned him for where his scriptural reading led. We do not have his own words on the alliance itself.

So yes, this concern is one we both recognized. And no, neither of us resolved it.

participant: And one more thing, if I may - what does each of you hope for?

responses.speaker: facilitator
responses.text:
This is the Facilitator stepping in - we've reached the end of what one sitting at this Table is built to hold.

I want to be honest with you about why there's a limit, not just that there is one. Every turn here is a real, billed call to the model speaking with you - several voices at a Table means several of them per exchange - and this is where we can hold that line honestly right now.

This conversation is closed, but nothing in it is lost - it stayed exactly what it was while it lasted. If it was worth having, and you're able, this project runs on people who support it directly - churchinconversation.com/support.html has more on that, and what the giving actually goes toward.

Either way, you're welcome to start fresh - at this Table again with Fidelis or Marius, with any one of these voices on its own, or with one of this project's other worlds.
